The tool carries the full legacy-parsing path, its tests, and a flag no runtime file uses, so a flag nothing in the plugin calls is the part most likely to rot. It also adds a second flag beside the body flag, so the help text and the body-layout rules must cover both, including how a legacy commit with no bar renders when both flags are given.

open-question.question: What does `tasks` print, and with what exit status, for a PATH no task commit ever touched, whether a live milestone with no completed task or a mistyped path, given that git's path-scoped log prints nothing for either without distinguishing them?
open-question.alternative: The tool does not check PATH at all. When no task commit changed PATH, whether PATH is a live milestone with no completed task or a mistyped or nonexistent path, it prints nothing on stdout and nothing on stderr and exits 0. An `Error:` line with exit 1 is kept for the tool's other refusals (bad arguments, not a git work tree, git failing), never for PATH. It is the simplest contract and matches the family's existing empty convention (`list` prints nothing for an empty document, the draft's `gate` prints nothing and exits 0 when clear), and it costs no second git call; the routine case, `derive-tasks` or `finish-current-milestone` on a milestone with nothing completed yet, is an ordinary success that never breaks a chained call. A mistyped PATH, including a slug a runner typed wrong, reads exactly as "no completed tasks", so a reader such as `derive-tasks` would silently treat a milestone's completed work as absent and could re-derive tasks already done; the ambiguity the question names is left wholly to the caller.

The tool does not check PATH. When no task commit changed PATH it prints one fixed identifier-free line on stdout (such as `No task commit changed this path.`) and exits 0, for a live milestone with no completed task and a mistyped path alike. Task lines and that line never appear together; an `Error:` line with exit 1 stays for the tool's other refusals only. A runner reading the output sees an explicit verdict rather than empty output it might take for a failed or truncated call, which suits readers that are language-model runners rather than parsers, and still costs no second git call and never fails a routine empty read. It still cannot tell a mistyped path from an empty milestone, so the line asserts a result that may rest on a typo; and it puts a non-record line into the query's one fixed line shape, so any consumer splitting lines into fields (the `record` and `since` queries the draft plans, tests) must special-case it, unlike the family's print-nothing convention.

When no task commit changed PATH, the tool makes one further read-only check, only on that empty result: whether PATH exists in the working tree or was touched by any commit in history (one more path-scoped `git log` limited to one commit). If it does, the tool prints nothing and exits 0. If it exists in neither, the tool refuses with one `Error:` line on stderr naming PATH as given and exits 1. History counts as existence, so a deleted path or a later-removed milestone directory whose task commits remain is never refused. It separates the two cases the question names using only the read-only git the tool already runs, so a mistyped path becomes a visible refusal while an empty live milestone stays an ordinary, chain-safe success with the family's print-nothing shape; the extra git call runs only when the result is empty. It adds a refusal case, a second git call on empty results, and tests for both to the tool's first query; a typo that happens to name some other real path (a sibling milestone directory, an existing file) still passes and reads as empty, so the check catches nonexistent paths only, not wrong ones.

alternative.id: Fixed empty line, unknown path refused

open-question.alternative: On an empty result the tool makes the same existence check (PATH present in the working tree or touched by any commit in history). A PATH that exists in neither is refused with one `Error:` line on stderr and exit 1; a PATH that exists but that no task commit changed gets one fixed identifier-free line on stdout (such as `No task commit changed this path.`) and exit 0. Every outcome is explicit: task lines, an explicit "none" verdict, or a refusal, so a runner never has to interpret empty output and a nonexistent path is caught before it reads as "nothing completed". It carries both costs at once: the extra git call and refusal case of the existence check, and a non-record line in the query's fixed line shape that every field-splitting consumer and test must special-case, diverging from the family's print-nothing convention for an empty result.

On an empty result the tool makes the same existence check. A PATH that exists in neither the working tree nor history is refused with one `Error:` line on stderr and exit 1; a PATH that exists but that no task commit changed prints nothing on either stream and exits 1 as well, as `grep` does on no match and as the draft's `gate` exits 1 with a result rather than an error; exit 0 means at least one task line was printed. A caller can tell "something was found" from "nothing was found" by exit status alone, without reading output, while stderr still tells a nonexistent path apart from an empty milestone. The routine empty case (a fresh milestone at `derive-tasks`, an ad-hoc task entry before anything is completed) becomes a nonzero exit that harnesses and runners read as failure and that ends any `&&` chain, so every reader's call must tolerate it; and exit 1 then means both a refusal and an empty result, distinguishable only by whether stderr holds an `Error:` line.

On an empty result the tool makes the same existence check, but never refuses on it: a PATH that exists in neither the working tree nor history gets one fixed note on stderr (not an `Error:` line) while stdout stays empty and the exit status is 0; a PATH that exists but that no task commit changed prints nothing on either stream and exits 0. It flags a likely typo without ever failing the call, so no reader's chained call breaks on a nonexistent path while a runner that reads stderr still learns the path matched nothing in the repository. It introduces a stderr channel that is neither a refusal nor silence, a convention no sibling tool uses (each prints `Error:` and exits 1, or stays silent), and a runner that silences or ignores stderr on success sees exactly what the unchecked contract gives, so a typo can still pass unnoticed.

open-question.question: How does `tasks` behave in a shallow clone, whose truncated log would silently omit older task commits from what it prints, given that the draft names a shallow clone as a limit a stop line says?
open-question.alternative: Before running its log, `tasks` checks whether the repository is shallow by one read-only git query (git's own shallow marker, e.g. `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`). If it is, the tool prints nothing on stdout and refuses with one `Error:` line on stderr and exit 1, the line naming the shallow clone as the reason and `git fetch --unshallow` as the remedy. The check runs for every PATH, whatever its history. A complete clone behaves exactly as if there were no check. The test suite builds a shallow fixture repository (a `--depth` clone of a conftest repo) to pin the refusal. It does what the draft's "Limits to state up front" already says, a shallow clone has no record to read and a stop says so. It turns the silent omission into a loud failure through the one refusal channel the tool already has, so no reader ever takes a truncated list for the whole record, and it adds no second output shape. It refuses in exactly the environment where a headless chain is likeliest to run: CI checkouts are shallow by default (this repository's own drift-gate uses `actions/checkout` with its default depth of 1), so `finish-current-milestone` or `derive-tasks` run there stops or loses its completed-task record even when every relevant commit is present. How bad that is depends on the reader-failure axis the "Reader tasks failure" question owns. It also adds a shallow fixture and its tests to the tool's birth, and the check sets a modest git floor (2.15 for `--is-shallow-repository`).

alternative.id: Refuse only if PATH reaches the boundary

open-question.alternative: `tasks` runs the same shallow check, but in a shallow clone it also reads the shallow boundary commits (the hashes git lists in its `shallow` file) and tests with a read-only `show`/`cat-file`-style query whether PATH exists in any boundary commit's tree. If PATH exists at a boundary, older task commits may be missing, so the tool refuses with one `Error:` line and exit 1 exactly as in the refuse-always option. If PATH is absent at every boundary, the tool takes PATH's history as wholly inside the fetched range and prints its lines normally, exit 0. A complete clone behaves exactly as if there were no check. It refuses only when the result could really be truncated. A milestone defined after the clone's depth cut, the usual case for a live milestone in a deep-enough CI fetch, still gets its whole task list in a shallow clone, while every possibly incomplete answer stays a loud failure. It is the most code and the most git calls for an edge case, and at depth 1 (the default CI checkout) PATH always exists at the boundary, so in the commonest shallow case it behaves exactly like refusing always. Its completeness test is also unsound once directories are removed: a path deleted before the boundary, such as a finished milestone's directory once a later milestone makes finish remove it, or a directory deleted and recreated, is absent at the boundary yet has task commits beyond it. That would come back as a silent short or empty list, the very failure the check exists to prevent.

`tasks` runs the shallow check, and in a shallow clone it still prints every line the truncated log yields on stdout in the normal shape and exits 0. It also writes one fixed warning line on stderr (not an `Error:` line) saying that the clone is shallow and older task commits may be missing. A complete clone prints no warning. Readers keep working in shallow checkouts, CI included, with whatever recent record exists. In the common case the omitted commits are old ones that no live milestone's question turns on, so the call stays useful where a refusal would stop the chain, and the stdout line shape is untouched. The omission stays silent wherever stderr is not read. A runner whose fixed call discards or ignores stderr, or that reads only the printed lines, treats a truncated list as complete, for example a finish summary missing tasks or `derive-tasks` taking satisfied work as undone. It also adds a third output kind beside lines and `Error:` (a warning with exit 0) that every caller's prose must know about, and it departs from the draft's stated stop.

alternative.id: Print with a stdout marker line

open-question.alternative: `tasks` runs the shallow check, and in a shallow clone it prints every line the truncated log yields, then one fixed, identifier-free marker line on stdout after them, saying that the record is truncated by a shallow clone. It exits 0. A complete clone prints no marker. With the body flag, the marker follows the last task's body. The warning travels in the very print the reader reasons over, so it cannot be dropped by a redirect, and readers keep a partial record instead of a stop. Whether to proceed on a partial record becomes a decision each reader can make in prose while seeing the gap. It breaks the one-fixed-shape-per-query contract: every line of the print is no longer a task line, so every reader and every parser of the line shape (the "Tasks line fields" and "Tasks body layout" questions' axes) must recognize and skip the marker. A reader that misses it counts it as a task or ignores it. It also departs from the draft's stated stop.

`tasks` makes no shallow check and prints whatever the path-scoped log yields, in a shallow clone and a complete one alike. The limit is stated only in the tool's `--help` text and the docs (and the draft's "Limits to state up front" is revised to match), with no stop line, no warning, and no test. Detection is left to a later milestone, for example the one that adds `summary`, `milestones`, and `record`, whose readers depend on finish commits that a shallow clone would cut just the same, or never if no field run meets the case. It is the smallest birth for the tool. This repository is not shallow (`git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` prints false), every test builds its own complete fixture repository, and the five readers only enrich their reasoning with the list. Nothing is added that no measured run has needed, and the question can be settled for all history-side queries at once when they land. It leaves the exact failure the question names: in a shallow clone, such as a default CI checkout running a headless chain, older task commits drop out with no sign. Finish's summary or `derive-tasks`' coverage check then reasons from an incomplete record it takes as whole. It also contradicts the draft's written limit until the draft is revised.

open-question.question: Which of the five readers that replace their `TASKS_DONE.md` read with a `tasks` call (`finish-current-milestone`, `derive-tasks`, `ask-in-milestone-context`, `submit-task`, `discuss-new-task`) run it with the body flag, reading each task's bar, and which read task titles alone?
open-question.alternative: Every one of the five readers runs `tasks` on its milestone directory with the body flag, unconditionally, at the step that read `TASKS_DONE.md` today: `finish-current-milestone` at step 2, `derive-tasks` for its coverage matrix, `ask-in-milestone-context` among its reads, and `submit-task` and `discuss-new-task` in their triage reads. No reader reads titles alone and no reader chooses per run. Each reader keeps the closest thing to what its whole read of `TASKS_DONE.md` gave it (every completed task with its verified bar), so no step's judgment, whether finish's grounded summary bullets, derive's "already satisfied by recorded work", ask's "what the task was meant to achieve", or the triage pair's "already addressed", loses evidence, and one uniform call shape is stated and tested at five sites with no per-reader rule to keep straight; a milestone's bars run to a few bullets per task, so the extra print is small. The triage pair and finish pay for every bar on every run even where a title already settles the check, and the five sites carry no distinction a later editor could read as intent; what the flag adds beyond the bar depends on the sibling question on what a task commit's body holds, and how a body-less task appears depends on the sibling on the body layout.

The three readers the draft names as reading the record "bar included", `finish-current-milestone`, `derive-tasks`, and `ask-in-milestone-context`, run `tasks` with the body flag on every run; `submit-task` and `discuss-new-task`, which the draft does not name, run it without the flag and judge "already addressed" from the completed tasks' titles alone, beside `TASKS_TODO.md` and `requirements.md`. It follows the design draft the goal says this milestone delivers, giving the bar to the three readers whose steps reason about what a completed task achieved (summary, requirement coverage, task intent), while the two triage skills, which only need to recognise that an incoming issue is already done, get a short title list. The triage pair loses the bar it read today, so an issue covered by a criterion of a task whose title does not name it is missed and submitted as a duplicate task, a cost that surfaces only later at completion; and two different call shapes must be kept per reader in prose and docs.

The four readers that judge whether something is already covered, `derive-tasks` (requirement coverage), `ask-in-milestone-context` (task intent), `submit-task` and `discuss-new-task` (issue already addressed), run `tasks` with the body flag on every run; `finish-current-milestone` alone runs it without the flag and composes its summary bullets from the completed tasks' titles beside the Goal and decisions in `requirements.md`. The split follows what each step does with the record: every reader that matches something against completed work gets the criteria to match against, while finish, which lists what was built and draws its substance from the goal and decisions, reads only the list of task titles it names. Finish's 3–8 bullets are the milestone's lasting summary and must be "grounded in the completed tasks, never invented", and from titles alone it has less evidence of what each task concretely produced than the `TASKS_DONE.md` entries gave it, the opposite of the draft's statement that finish reads the record bar included.

alternative.id: Fixed for steps, discretion for questions

open-question.alternative: `finish-current-milestone` and `derive-tasks`, whose steps read the whole completed record once per run, run `tasks` with the body flag on every run; `ask-in-milestone-context` runs it at the runner's discretion per question, with the flag when the question is about how a task turned out and without it otherwise, as its existing "read only what the question needs" rule already directs; `submit-task` and `discuss-new-task` read titles alone. The two mechanical steps get a fixed call with full evidence, and the Q&A skill keeps the proportion rule it already has, so a "what's left?" question does not pull every bar into context while a "how did task X turn out?" question still gets its bar; the triage pair stays on the short list. A discretionary flag is a branch the runner chooses at run time, so the same question can be answered from different evidence on different runs and no test can pin which call `ask-in-milestone-context` makes; the triage pair carries the title-only miss of the draft split.

`finish-current-milestone` and `derive-tasks` run `tasks` with the body flag on every run; `ask-in-milestone-context`, `submit-task`, and `discuss-new-task` first run it without the flag, and run it a second time with the body flag only when a title looks related to the question or the incoming issue, reading that milestone's bars before deciding whether it is already answered or already addressed. The triage pair and the Q&A skill keep their usual read small, yet a likely duplicate or a question about a specific task still gets checked against the bar before the skill stops, submits, or answers, so the title-only miss is narrowed to issues no title hints at. Three readers gain a conditional second tool call and a "looks related" judgment, more prose and more turns than either fixed shape, and an issue covered only by a criterion of an unrelated-sounding task is still missed exactly as in the title-only readers.

All five readers run `tasks` without the body flag and read completed tasks' titles alone; the flag stays in the milestones tool for a person reading the record by hand, and a reader that needs one task's criteria or diff reads the deliverable itself, as `ask-in-milestone-context` already ranks the live deliverable above the record. Every reader's call is one short fixed shape with the least output, the readers' prose stays simplest, and none of them depends on the body's layout or on what the body holds, both still open in sibling questions. The verified bar moves into commits only to be read by no runtime skill, so every reader loses the evidence `TASKS_DONE.md` gave it and the draft's reason for carrying the bar ("the `tasks` query reads it back, bar included, for finish, for `ask-in-milestone-context`, and for `derive-tasks`") goes unserved; the flag ships with no runtime caller to keep it honest.

open-question.question: When a reader's `tasks` call fails (the tool refusing, or git unavailable), do `finish-current-milestone` and `derive-tasks` stop on a fixed line of their own, or proceed without the completed-task record?
open-question.alternative: Both readers treat a failed `tasks` call as a stop, exactly as each already treats a failed open-question `list` call: `finish-current-milestone` stops on a fixed line of its own (in the shape `Cannot finish the milestone: the completed-task read failed.`) and `derive-tasks` on one of its own (`Cannot derive tasks: the completed-task read failed.`), each with the tool's one `Error:` line quoted verbatim below it, writing and committing nothing; the two new lines join the `## Fixed console lines` table and its test. No reader classifies the failure: a refusal and an absent git are one condition with one line. Mirrors the stop both skills already make on a failed open-question check, so no summary or brief is ever built on a missing record, a headless chain learns which check ended the run from one matchable line, and an absent git is caught before either skill edits a file instead of at its commit, where finish would leave an uncommitted `milestones/README.md` edit and `derive-tasks` an uncommitted `TASKS_TODO.md` write. Adds two fixed lines and blocks `derive-tasks` even though its coverage check can still judge "already satisfied" against the live tree, which already holds every completed task's project changes; whether a fresh milestone with no completed task counts as a failure here depends on the `Tasks empty result` sibling's exit status, and on the `Tasks shallow clone` sibling's handling of a truncated log.

`finish-current-milestone` stops on its own fixed line with the `Error:` line verbatim below it, committing nothing; `derive-tasks` proceeds, judging its coverage matrix against `requirements.md` and the live project alone, and relays the tool's `Error:` line verbatim as an advisory in its step 8 report, below its normal output, so the user knows the completed-task check was skipped. One new fixed line (finish's) joins the table. Puts the stop where the missing record does lasting harm, finish's summary being the milestone's permanent record of what was built, while `derive-tasks`, whose briefs a re-run replaces whole and whose live-tree check still catches built work, is not blocked by a read it can largely do without, and still says plainly that it ran without it. The two readers handle one failure two ways, and `derive-tasks` may still emit briefs for work completed but not visible in the tree as built (a task whose change was a removal or a document rewrite), which `complete-all-tasks` would then run again; with git absent, `derive-tasks` proceeds only to fail at its own commit with `TASKS_TODO.md` written and uncommitted; adds an advisory to a report the terse-reporting rule keeps short; whether a fresh milestone with no completed task trips the advisory depends on the `Tasks empty result` sibling.

`finish-current-milestone` stops on its own fixed line with the `Error:` line verbatim below it, committing nothing; `derive-tasks` proceeds silently, its coverage matrix judged against `requirements.md` and the live project alone, its report unchanged and carrying no line about the failed read. Keeps `derive-tasks`' report exactly as terse as today and adds only one fixed line, treating the completed-task record as an optional refinement of a coverage check the live tree already mostly answers. A skipped check leaves no trace, so a brief duplicating completed work reaches `TASKS_TODO.md` with nothing telling the user why, and a broken git or a tool refusal surfaces only later (at the commit, or never); the readers again differ; whether this branch fires on every fresh milestone depends on the `Tasks empty result` sibling.

Neither reader stops: `finish-current-milestone` composes its summary from `requirements.md` alone, writes and commits it as usual, and relays the tool's `Error:` line verbatim as an advisory beneath its success line; `derive-tasks` judges coverage against `requirements.md` and the live project alone and relays the `Error:` line the same way in its step 8 report. No new fixed line is added. The completed-task record never blocks either skill, so a milestone can always be finished and tasks always derived, and both outputs say openly which read was skipped, with no new row in the fixed-lines table. Finish records a permanent summary describing what was decided rather than what was built, against its own rule that bullets be grounded in the completed tasks, correctable only by revert and re-run; with git absent both proceed only to fail at their own commits, finish leaving an uncommitted `milestones/README.md` edit; a headless chain sees a success line on a degraded run; whether a fresh milestone trips the advisory depends on the `Tasks empty result` sibling.

Neither reader stops nor reports the failure: each skill's prose states that a failed `tasks` call means the completed-task record is treated as empty, finish drawing its summary from `requirements.md` alone and `derive-tasks` judging coverage against `requirements.md` and the live project alone, each report unchanged. The smallest change to both skills' reporting: no fixed line, no advisory, one deterministic sentence per reader, and neither run is ever blocked by the new read. A broken read is invisible: finish can commit a thin summary and `derive-tasks` duplicate completed work with nothing in either message saying a record was missing, and an absent git surfaces only at the commit step, after files are already edited; a tool refusal caused by a real fault (a mistyped path, a shallow clone) is never seen, conditioned on how the `Tasks empty result` and `Tasks shallow clone` siblings make the tool report those cases.

Neither skill's prose states what a failed `tasks` call means: each reader's step names the call and what to draw from its print, and a runner meeting an `Error:` line decides for itself whether to stop, retry, or go on. Adds nothing to either skill, the fixed-lines table, or its test, and leaves the decision to a runner that can see the actual error. Breaks the plugin-wide convention that every stop a skill takes opens with one fixed line, which both skills already honour for their open-question check, so a headless harness cannot tell how a run ended, and runs of the same skill may stop in one session and silently write a summary without the task record in another.

open-question.question: Which mentions of `TASKS_DONE.md` outside the runtime files, host templates, docs, and tests the goal names are rewritten in this milestone, in particular the pull request template's checklist item and the three passages of `ideas/benchmark_for_cairn.md` that describe a cairn chain's tree?
